title: Every Named Concept in the Book
banner: Every Named Concept in the Book

lead.text: *A working glossary with definitions, examples, and cross-references.*

This section gathers every named concept, tool, framework, and technique used in the book — organized alphabetically, with a short definition, one specific example, and a cross-reference to where the concept is developed in depth.
Use this section as a quick reference before a difficult moment. If you remember the name but not the specifics, this is where to look.
Entries in bold are ones this book explicitly names and treats. Italicized entries are supporting concepts referenced throughout.

blocks.text:
The practice of retrieving information from memory rather than re-reading it. One of the most effective known techniques for durable learning.
*Example: Instead of re-reading a chapter, close the book and try to write down its main points from memory.*
See: Deep Dive 3 — Learning How to Learn

The neuroscience finding that verbally naming an emotion reduces its physiological intensity. Basis of the 'name what you feel' practice.
*Example: Saying 'I am anxious about this meeting' silently to yourself measurably reduces the anxiety, more than trying to suppress it.*
See: Lesson 1.2 — Naming What You Feel

The cognitive bias in which the first number or reference point in a discussion disproportionately shapes all subsequent estimates.
*Example: The first salary number mentioned in a negotiation usually determines the final range of the outcome, regardless of its rational basis.*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases; Lesson 4.5 — Negotiation

Ibn Khaldun's term for group solidarity or cohesion — the invisible force that determines whether coalitions prevail regardless of individual talent.
*Example: A cohesive small team of moderate performers regularly beats a group of stars with weak coordination.*
See: Masters Deep Card — Ibn Khaldun; Lesson 4.6

Sophie Leroy's finding that switching between tasks leaves part of your attention on the previous task for 20+ minutes.
*Example: You cannot 'quickly check email' and return to focused work at full capacity — a significant fraction of your attention stays on email for the next 20 minutes.*
See: Lesson 1.3 — The Attention Audit

The tendency to judge probability by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by actual base rates.
*Example: Overestimating the risk of dying in a plane crash because they make headlines; underestimating the risk of dying in a car accident because they don't.*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases

Recurring feature in this book. A scenario in which the ordinary lesson has to be executed under adversarial conditions — anger, time pressure, missing information, or public failure.
*Example: Practicing 'The Pause' when someone is publicly attacking you in a client meeting.*
See: Every Level

entries.title: BATNA (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement)

blocks.text:
Fisher and Ury's term for your best fallback if the current negotiation fails. Determines your true leverage.
*Example: In salary negotiation, your BATNA is the strongest other offer you could realistically accept. A specific, verified BATNA transforms your negotiating stance.*
See: Lesson 4.5 — Negotiation

Communication principle: state the conclusion or recommendation first, then supporting reasoning.
*Example: In an email to a busy executive, the first sentence states the recommendation; the rest provides context.*
See: Lesson 4.2 — Communicating Under Pressure

This book's term for the end-of-level integration scenario that tests all skills from that level under pressure.
*Example: Level 4's Boss Fight ('The Difficult Room') integrates listening, communication, difficult conversations, and reading power dynamics simultaneously.*
See: End of each Level; Boss Fight Debrief Archive

Herbert Simon's insight that humans and organizations cannot maximize because of limits on information, attention, and time. Foundation of satisficing.
*Example: You cannot fully evaluate every job offer against every possible alternative — you satisfice within your cognitive bounds.*
See: Deep Card — Herbert Simon; Level 7

The practice of forecasting in probability ranges that reflect actual epistemic uncertainty, then tracking whether the ranges hold up over time.
*Example: Saying 'I'd give it 70% odds' rather than 'it'll probably work' — and then, months later, checking whether 70% of your 70% forecasts came true.*
See: Lesson 7.3 — Probabilistic Thinking

Immanuel Kant's principle: act only according to principles you could will to be universal law.
*Example: 'If I would not want everyone to lie in this situation, I should not lie in it.'*
See: Lesson 8.5 — Moral Choices

This book's six-part prompt framework for AI: Context, Goal, Constraints, Examples, Output format, Verification.
*Example: A CGCEO-V prompt for salary negotiation prep is dramatically more useful than 'help me negotiate my salary.'*
See: Lesson 6.1 — AI Collaboration; Prompt Library

A short, memorable, evidence-based list of steps or checks used to prevent predictable errors of cognitive overload. Three types: DO-CONFIRM, READ-DO, IF-THEN.
*Example: Surgical checklists cut surgical death rates measurably in WHO studies. Same principle applies to any complex professional workflow.*
See: Lesson 5.2 — Checklists

Warren Buffett's term for the domain within which your judgment is reliable. Staying inside it and knowing where its edges lie.
*Example: You may be excellent at evaluating consumer products and terrible at evaluating biotech — knowing which is which is more valuable than being good at both.*
See: Deep Card — Warren Buffett

This book's sequence for figuring out unfamiliar situations: Calm, Observe, Define, Alternatives, Rank, Act, Adapt.
*Example: Applied to being stranded in a foreign city with no working card and a flight in six hours.*
See: Lesson 3.4 — Figuring It Out When No One Knows

The mathematical principle that small consistent gains multiply over time — applied to skills, reputation, relationships, and financial outcomes.
*Example: A 1% weekly improvement compounds to a 68% improvement over 52 weeks. This applies to habits, not just interest rates.*
See: Level 8.6 — Long-Term Thinking; Financial Deep Dive

The tendency to notice and remember evidence that supports what you already believe, while ignoring contradicting evidence.
*Example: Reading a report about a candidate you like and finding it 'clearly positive' — while a similar report about a candidate you don't like reads as 'clearly concerning.'*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases

This book's structured scenario format in which each possible move is followed through its downstream consequences — what was gained, what was missed, what you should have noticed.
*Example: The 15 branching scenarios in the Consequence Engine section demonstrate this format at length.*
See: The Consequence Engine — What Would You Do?

This book's practice of pairing every named bias with a specific question that, when asked, tends to counteract it.
*Example: For anchoring: 'If I hadn't heard the first number, what would I have proposed?'*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases

This book's seven-question framework for making consequential decisions: what I want, what I know, what I'm assuming, what my options are, what could go wrong, what happens next, what I should choose.
*Example: Applied to a career-change decision, in writing, with 24 hours of sleep between reaching the answer and acting on it.*
See: Lesson 7.1 — The Decision 7

The practice of recording consequential decisions at the time they are made — with reasoning, expected outcome, and review date — for later honest comparison against actual outcomes.
*Example: Reviewing a job-change decision six months later, against the reasoning you documented at the time, reveals patterns hindsight bias would otherwise erase.*
See: Lesson 7.6 — The Decision Journal

Cal Newport's term for the ability to concentrate without distraction on a cognitively demanding task. The 90-minute block is this book's practical version.
*Example: One 90-minute deep-work block per workday, with phone in another room, produces more meaningful output than eight hours of fragmented time.*
See: Lesson 1.3 — The Attention Audit

K. Anders Ericsson's term for the specific kind of practice that builds expertise: at the edge of current ability, with immediate feedback, focused on specific weaknesses.
*Example: Presenting to a video camera, watching the recording, identifying the 30 seconds that were weakest, and drilling that specific weakness.*
See: Deep Dive 3 — Learning How to Learn

The practice of arguing against your own position seriously, or having someone else do so, to expose weaknesses in your thinking.
*Example: Before committing to a plan, spend 30 minutes writing out the strongest case against it. Note whether any of the arguments actually shift your view.*
See: Lesson 2.5 — First Principles; Lesson 7.5 — Pre-Mortem

Socrates's method of asking questions that expose the incoherence of confidently-held beliefs.
*Example: In a meeting where someone claims certainty about a market prediction, asking 'How would we know if we were wrong?' is elenchus applied.*
See: Deep Card — Socrates; Lesson 2.4

Lisa Feldman Barrett's term for the ability to distinguish emotions with precision — more specific words for what you feel.
*Example: People with high granularity distinguish 'frustrated because a project stalled' from 'disappointed because I was hoping for recognition' — and respond differently to each.*
See: Lesson 1.2 — Naming What You Feel

Greg McKeown's principle: 'the disciplined pursuit of less.' Not doing more, but doing fewer, more important things.
*Example: Warren Buffett's (attributed) 25/5 rule — list 25 goals, do the top 5, actively avoid the other 20 — is essentialism applied.*
See: Lesson 5.1 — The Top Three Rule

Aristotle's term for human flourishing — a good life, well-lived, produced by consistent virtuous action over time.
*Example: Not a mood or a feeling — a durable state of a life spent well, visible only in retrospect.*
See: Deep Card — Aristotle; Level 8

In systems thinking, a mechanism by which a change in one variable feeds back to affect the same variable — reinforcing (amplifying) or balancing (stabilizing).
*Example: A team's declining morale reduces productivity, which attracts negative feedback from leadership, which further reduces morale — a reinforcing loop.*
See: Deep Dive 1 — Systems Thinking

The learning method of explaining a concept to a hypothetical novice, noticing where you stumble, and drilling on those specific gaps.
*Example: If you cannot explain first-principles reasoning to a teenager without using jargon, you don't yet understand it.*
See: Lesson 3.1 — Skill Sprint; Deep Dive 3

This book's term for a real-world assignment that closes a lesson — done in the actual world, not on paper, this week.
*Example: 'Ask a genuine four-line help request this week to someone whose input you actually need.'*
See: End of many lessons

Reasoning up from what MUST be true (irreducible physical, mathematical, or empirical facts) rather than from received wisdom or analogy.
*Example: Elon Musk's public application to rocket-launch cost structure — deriving the cost of raw materials and asking why launches cost so much more.*
See: Lesson 2.5 — First Principles Thinking

Taiichi Ohno's Toyota technique of asking 'why?' five times in succession to reach a root cause of a problem.
*Example: The onboarding is slow. Why? Because IT provisioning takes days. Why? Because there's no automated ticket. Why? Because… and so on.*
See: Lesson 5.4 — Fix the Broken Process

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's term for the state of complete absorption in an activity — one of the most reliable sources of subjective well-being.
*Example: The 90 minutes you spent writing yesterday and didn't notice time passing.*
See: Level 8.4 — Where Meaning Lives

This book's four-category tagging system for claims: Fact, Story, Inference, Opinion.
*Example: Tagging every sentence of a colleague's urgent report silently reveals how much of the perceived crisis is fact vs. narrative.*
See: Lesson 2.2 — Facts vs. Stories vs. Inferences vs. Opinions

Toyota's principle: 'go and see.' Understand the situation by physically observing where the work happens.
*Example: A support process cannot be improved from the meeting room. It must be improved by sitting with a support agent as they handle real tickets.*
See: Lesson 5.4; Level 5 Boss Fight

This book's recurring feature: a synthesis of relevant historical thinkers' views on a specific problem, with explicit acknowledgment of where they might be wrong.
*Example: For a difficult conversation: what would Chris Voss notice, what would Stone-Patton-Heen suggest, what would Marcus Aurelius warn against.*
See: Every major lesson; Masters Deep Cards

Angela Duckworth's term for sustained interest and effort toward long-term goals — a stronger predictor of long-term success than raw talent.
*Example: The Resourceful Human's willingness to keep working on hard problems past the point where casual talent would quit.*
See: Deep Card — Angela Duckworth

Carol Dweck's frame: the belief that ability is developed through effort, rather than fixed at birth. Correlates with better learning and resilience.
*Example: 'I don't know this YET' is growth-mindset framing. 'I'm not good at this' is fixed-mindset framing.*
See: Deep Card — Carol Dweck

BJ Fogg's technique of attaching a new habit to an existing habit that reliably happens: 'After I [X], I will [Y].'
*Example: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I will write down three things I want to accomplish today.'*
See: Lesson 1.5 — Habits That Survive Bad Weeks

The cognitive bias in which one strong impression of a person or thing colors judgments of unrelated attributes.
*Example: A candidate who presents impressively is over-credited on unrelated dimensions like strategic thinking.*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases

The tendency to feel that an outcome was obvious after it occurred, obscuring the actual uncertainty at the time of the decision.
*Example: 'Of course that deal fell through — the signs were all there.' They weren't obvious before the failure.*
See: Lesson 2.3; Lesson 7.6 — Decision Journal

'It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law.' A self-referential caution about project estimation.
*Example: The 6-month project that ends up taking 11 months, even after adding a buffer.*
See: Lesson 5.5 — Project Planning

In negotiation: proposing conditional concessions linked to specific reciprocal moves from the other side.
*Example: 'If you can meet me at \$100k, I can accept a November 1 start.' Ties flexibility to specific reciprocity.*
See: Lesson 4.5 — Negotiation

Eisenhower's framework, adapted here: rate every task on impact (1-3) and urgency (1-3), multiply, sort. The top three are your Top Three.
*Example: A one-hour weekly ritual that transforms task lists from noise into a working plan.*
See: Lesson 5.1 — The Top Three Rule

Peter Gollwitzer's research finding that pre-committing to specific IF-THEN behavior dramatically improves follow-through vs. general resolutions.
*Example: 'When I sit down at my desk in the morning, I will write for 20 minutes before opening email.' — outperforms 'I want to write more.'*
See: Boss Fight Debrief — The Big Decision

Learning technique of mixing different but related topics in a single study session — harder in the moment, better for long-term retention.
*Example: Studying three related concepts in rotation, rather than one at a time, produces stronger retention when tested weeks later.*
See: Deep Dive 3 — Learning How to Learn

Charlie Munger's technique: solve problems by asking what would guarantee failure — and avoid those specifically.
*Example: Instead of 'how do we succeed at this launch,' ask 'what would guarantee it fails?' The list often reveals more actionable insights.*
See: Deep Card — Charlie Munger; Lesson 7.5 — Pre-Mortem

Confucius's term for the noble or exemplary person — one who cultivates virtue through daily practice rather than by title or inheritance.
*Example: The colleague who consistently does the right thing in small ways, whether or not anyone is watching.*
See: Deep Card — Confucius

The Japanese principle (associated with Taiichi Ohno and Toyota) of continuous incremental improvement by the people who do the work.
*Example: A support team meeting once a week to identify one small improvement they can make in their own process, then doing it, then meeting again.*
See: Lesson 5.4 — Process Improvement

This book's three-part listening practice: Listen fully, Mirror 3-5 of their last words, Reflect the underlying issue in one sentence.
*Example: In a heated meeting, mirroring 'losing the deal' back to the speaker often produces the specific elaboration you needed.*
See: Lesson 4.1 — Listening Like a Professional

Viktor Frankl's therapeutic school based on the search for meaning as the primary motivational force.
*Example: Asking not 'what can I get from life' but 'what is life asking of me here' — the frame Frankl developed in Auschwitz and used for the rest of his career.*
See: Deep Card — Viktor Frankl

Kahneman and Tversky's finding that losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel pleasant.
*Example: Refusing a small risk with an expected value gain because the possibility of loss is emotionally more salient than the expected upside.*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases; Level 7

This book's three-step process improvement approach: map the actual current process, measure where it breaks, move one specific step.
*Example: Fixing a slow onboarding by first drawing the actual flow, then measuring which step delays it most, then changing that one step.*
See: Lesson 5.4 — Fix the Broken Process

The private journal of Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor. Never intended for publication; the most durable personal-operating-system document ever written.
*Example: Book IV of the Meditations, read one entry per morning, changes how the rest of the day unfolds.*
See: Deep Card — Marcus Aurelius

Charlie Munger's term for a latticework of cross-disciplinary concepts used together to reason about complex problems.
*Example: Applying supply-and-demand (economics), incentives (psychology), and feedback loops (systems theory) to understand why an internal process keeps failing.*
See: Deep Card — Charlie Munger

Chris Voss's negotiation technique: repeat the last 3-5 words of the other person's sentence, with slight upward inflection. Invites elaboration.
*Example: 'The deal is going to fall through.' 'The deal is going to fall through?' Usually produces the specific concern underneath the general statement.*
See: Lesson 4.1 — Listening; Lesson 4.5 — Negotiation

Japanese term (used in Lean methodology) for waste — any activity that does not add value from the customer's perspective.
*Example: The 30-minute internal approval meeting for a decision that could have been made unilaterally by the person closest to the customer.*
See: Lesson 5.4 — Process Improvement

James Clear's rule: missing one day of a habit is human; missing two in a row is the start of a different habit — the habit of not doing it.
*Example: You skip the workout on Monday due to an emergency. You go on Tuesday. The habit survives.*
See: Lesson 1.5 — Habits That Survive Bad Weeks

The ethical check: would you be comfortable if this decision, and your reasoning for it, appeared on the front page of a newspaper tomorrow?
*Example: A moment of hesitation on any decision is often the newspaper test operating below the conscious level.*
See: Lesson 8.5 — Moral Choices

Marshall Rosenberg's four-part framework: observation, feeling, need, request. In that order.
*Example: 'When you cancelled our meeting without notice [observation], I felt disrespected [feeling] — I need predictability to plan my day [need]. Could we agree on 24 hours' notice for future changes? [request]'*
See: Level 4 — Communication

Jeff Bezos's distinction: reversible decisions (two-way doors) can be made fast; irreversible ones (one-way doors) deserve more time.
*Example: Choosing a font for a report: two-way. Deciding to have a child: one-way. Match effort to reversibility.*
See: Lesson 7.2 — Reversibility

Nassim Taleb's concept: the value of preserving future choices, especially when the costs of preservation are low and the potential upsides are large.
*Example: Continuing to have exploratory conversations with other companies even while happy in your current role preserves optionality at almost no cost.*
See: Deep Card — Nassim Taleb; Consequence Engine #1

The rhetorical trick of using passive constructions to hide agency. 'Mistakes were made' vs. 'I made mistakes.'
*Example: Every corporate apology written in passive voice signals evasion; every direct 'I did this' signals ownership.*
See: Deep Dive 2 — Communication Craft

This book's foundational technique: the deliberate insertion of two seconds between provocation and response, using breath and physical intervention.
*Example: The two-second pause between reading an activating email and typing a reply — where the difference between a career mistake and a professional response actually lives.*
See: Lesson 1.1 — The Pause

Martin Seligman's five-component model of flourishing: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment.
*Example: The weakest of the five is where to invest first. Ignoring one dimension entirely predicts subjective dissatisfaction over time regardless of achievement in others.*
See: Lesson 8.4 — Where Meaning Lives

Aristotle's term for practical wisdom — the ability to make good judgments in specific situations, as distinct from theoretical knowledge (sophia).
*Example: The senior professional who knows what to do in a novel situation — even without having seen it before — has phronesis. Textbook knowledge alone does not produce it.*
See: Deep Card — Aristotle; Level 8.1

Gary Klein's technique: at the start of a project, imagine it is one year later and the project has failed catastrophically. Write the postmortem for the failure that hasn't happened yet.
*Example: Teams that pre-mortem catch roughly 20-30% more risks than teams that just brainstorm risks.*
See: Lesson 7.5 — Pre-Mortem and Red Team

This book's communication structure: Point, Reason, Example, Point. Load-bearing content up front.
*Example: In a 45-second elevator update, PREP produces a memorable version of what would otherwise be a rambled two-minute answer.*
See: Lesson 4.2 — Communicating Under Pressure

Fisher and Ury's four-principle framework: separate people from problem, focus on interests not positions, invent options for mutual gain, insist on objective criteria.
*Example: The five-column negotiation prep is principled negotiation applied to your specific situation.*
See: Lesson 4.5 — Negotiation

The practice of forecasting in ranges rather than point estimates, and holding beliefs with calibrated confidence.
*Example: 'I'd give this project a 70% chance of shipping on time' — with the willingness to update as new evidence appears.*
See: Lesson 7.3 — Probabilistic Thinking

This book's five-line problem statement: symptom, context, underlying question, success criterion, first question to investigate.
*Example: Before writing the JD for a new hire, the 5-level problem statement reveals whether you have a capacity, prioritization, skills, or process problem.*
See: Lesson 2.1 — Define the Problem

This book's five diagnostic categories for what is actually driving avoidance: fear, boredom, confusion, resentment, shame.
*Example: Different flavors need different interventions. Fear-procrastination responds to lowering stakes; confusion-procrastination responds to studying examples.*
See: Lesson 1.6 — Procrastination Without Shame

Kim Scott's principle: care personally AND challenge directly. Missing either produces damage.
*Example: Care without challenge = ruinous empathy (feel-good, no growth). Challenge without care = obnoxious aggression (growth-inducing at unacceptable cost).*
See: Lesson 4.4 — Feedback

The cognitive bias in which the most recent event or period disproportionately weights our judgment.
*Example: Judging a colleague's overall performance by their last two weeks — ignoring the previous 50.*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases

The practice of assigning people the specific role of finding weaknesses in a plan — not to disagree, but to test.
*Example: Before committing to a major strategy, giving three colleagues one week to attack it — with time to prepare, and specific questions to answer.*
See: Lesson 7.5 — Pre-Mortem and Red Team

Jeff Bezos's decision technique: project forward to 80-year-old you, and ask which choice you'd regret least.
*Example: Especially useful for one-way-door decisions where the current uncertainty overwhelms rational analysis.*
See: Lesson 7.1 — The Decision 7

The property of a decision that determines how much effort to spend on it — reversible decisions should be fast, irreversible ones slow.
*Example: Choosing what to eat for lunch: fully reversible; quitting your job to found a startup: less reversible; who to marry: essentially not.*
See: Lesson 7.2 — One-Way and Two-Way Doors

Herbert Simon's term for accepting the first option that meets your criteria, rather than continuing to search for the theoretically optimal one. Won him a Nobel Prize.
*Example: Buying the second decent apartment you view, that meets your criteria, rather than viewing 40 more to find the theoretically best one.*
See: Deep Card — Herbert Simon; Lesson 3.5 — Knowing When to Stop

This book's feedback structure: Situation, Behavior, Impact, Inquiry into intent.
*Example: 'In yesterday's client meeting, when you interrupted Priya three times, the client seemed to lose their thread — what were you trying to do?'*
See: Lesson 4.4 — Feedback

Anticipating not just the direct consequences of a decision, but the consequences of those consequences — two rounds forward.
*Example: A price cut generates more sales (first order). Which strains capacity, degrades customer experience, and eventually loses customers (second order).*
See: Deep Dive 1 — Systems Thinking; Lesson 7.1

This book's 30/45/15 protocol for acquiring the operational level of a new skill in 90 minutes: 30 understand, 45 practice, 15 teach.
*Example: Learning enough about a new software tool to be operational for tomorrow's workshop, in one focused evening.*
See: Lesson 3.1 — The 90-Minute Skill Sprint

The learning technique of reviewing material at expanding intervals — dramatically better for long-term retention than massed practice.
*Example: Learning vocabulary via a spaced-repetition app produces retention months later that six hours of concentrated study in a single day cannot.*
See: Deep Dive 3 — Learning How to Learn

Ancient philosophical school (Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Seneca) emphasizing the distinction between what is and isn't in our control, and focusing effort on the first.
*Example: The Pause, naming what you feel, the discipline of response over reaction — all Stoic practices translated into modern professional life.*
See: Level 1; Level 8; Deep Cards — Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Seneca

The cognitive tendency to continue investing in something because of what you've already invested, rather than based on forward-looking value.
*Example: Finishing a bad book because you're already halfway through. Staying in a role because you've been there three years and 'need to make it work.'*
See: Lesson 2.3 — The Ten Biases

Philip Tetlock's research finding: the best forecasters (top ~2%) are not smarter than average, but they update their probabilities in small increments, avoid extremes, and treat their views as hypotheses.
*Example: The colleague who says '70%' rather than 'definitely' — and then, weeks later, says '55%' when new information arrives — is superforecasting in practice.*
See: Deep Card — Philip Tetlock; Level 7

Daniel Kahneman's frame from Thinking, Fast and Slow: System 1 is fast, intuitive, pattern-matching. System 2 is slow, deliberate, effortful.
*Example: System 1 drafts the reactive reply. System 2 catches it if you pause long enough to invite it.*
See: Deep Card — Daniel Kahneman; Level 2

The discipline of seeing wholes rather than parts — understanding feedback loops, bottlenecks, delays, and unintended consequences.
*Example: A team's declining performance is rarely a personnel issue and usually a systems issue — feedback loops, constraints, incentives.*
See: Deep Dive 1 — Systems Thinking

Chris Voss's phrase for understanding the other side's perspective as a professional discipline (not as a personality trait or moral virtue).
*Example: Labeling a client's frustration out loud — 'It sounds like you're worried about renewal risk' — usually reduces the frustration by a measurable amount within seconds.*
See: Lesson 4.1 — Listening; Deep Card — Chris Voss

Eli Goldratt's system-improvement framework: every system has ONE binding constraint at a time. Improvements elsewhere are wasted.
*Example: Improving your ability to write faster does not increase your team's output if the bottleneck is actually approval delays elsewhere.*
See: Deep Dive 1 — Systems Thinking

This book's rule: pick three things per week that, if done, would matter more than anything else. Book them into your calendar and defend them.
*Example: The Sunday 30 review that transforms next week's task list from noise into a working plan.*
See: Lesson 5.1 — The Top Three Rule

James Clear's principle: every habit has a 2-minute version that still counts. Design habits to survive bad days by making the minimum viable version impossibly small.
*Example: 'Meditate for two minutes' — even on days when you cannot imagine doing 20. The identity is what compounds, not the daily volume.*
See: Lesson 1.5 — Habits That Survive Bad Weeks

Anne Lamott's principle: the first draft of anything should be deliberately unpolished. Editing bad prose is easier than facing the blank page.
*Example: The report you needed to write got done because you wrote a 500-word deliberately-bad version first, then edited it into what you actually needed.*
See: Lesson 1.6 — Procrastination

This book's graduation assessment: a realistic scenario with incomplete information, competing stakeholders, and no clear framework. You are assessed on demonstrated behavior, not on which framework you apply.
*Example: Six weeks to fix a struggling department, with no clear map of what 'fixed' means or which reports to trust.*
See: The Final Unknown, in the main appendices

The annual practice of comparing your stated values against your revealed values — where your time and money actually go.
*Example: You say you value family. Your last month's calendar shows 60 hours a week at work and 6 with family. Which set of values are you actually living?*
See: Lesson 8.2 — Choose Your Values on Purpose

John Rawls's thought experiment: if you did not know which role you would play in a situation, would you still endorse this arrangement or decision?
*Example: If you didn't know whether you'd be the founder or the earliest employee, would you still structure this compensation split this way?*
See: Lesson 8.5 — Moral Choices

This book's discipline: every AI-generated citation, number, or current-state claim must be cross-checked against an independent primary source before consequential use.
*Example: The lawyer who cited six hallucinated cases in a brief — a real 2023 case — is the archetypal consequence of skipping verification.*
See: Lesson 6.3 — Verifying AI

Aristotle's central ethical insight: you become courageous by acting courageously, patient by acting patiently — until the acting becomes who you are.
*Example: The one-virtue-per-month practice from Franklin, translated into modern professional life.*
See: Lesson 8.3; Deep Card — Aristotle, Ben Franklin

This book's format for scenarios that present a situation, invite you to decide before reading on, then walk through the outcomes of each possible move.
*Example: The 15 scenarios in the Consequence Engine section demonstrate the format at length.*
See: The Consequence Engine

Knowing what matters. Distinguishable from knowledge (knowing what), intelligence (reasoning ability), and judgment (choosing well within a domain).
*Example: The senior operator who knows not only how to solve a problem, but whether it is the right problem to solve.*
See: Level 8.1

This book's final ethical filter: Truth (is it true?), Consequences (what happens next?), Character (who am I becoming?), Meaning (does this actually matter?).
*Example: Applied to any consequential decision — professional, personal, or moral — before acting.*
See: Final Wisdom Test, in the main appendices
This index is designed to be consulted, not read cover to cover. When you find yourself in a situation and think 'there was a name for this…' — this is the reference.

The concepts here are not just this book's inventions. Some are — CGCEO-V, CODA-R, FSIO, LMR, PREP, SBI-I, the Decision 7, the Top Three Rule. But many are older, better ideas synthesized from traditions worth respecting. The names matter less than the underlying practices.

Learn a small number of these well. Practice them under real conditions. Return to the index when you need a refresher. Over years, the vocabulary you have here compounds into the professional you become.
REMEMBER THIS
*“The vocabulary is not the practice. The practice is the practice. But naming it makes it faster to return to.”*
